PROP
2
INCREASES STATE’S RAINY DAY FUND. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 2
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2 TO PROTECT SCHOOLS, HEALTHCARE, PUBLIC SAFETY AND CALIFORNIA'S FINANCIAL FUTURE.
California's Rainy Day Fund, established by voters in 2014, was built for exactly this moment: an economy that swung our state budget from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.
Proposition 2 strengthens that fund, so schools, healthcare, and public safety don't pay the price for Sacramento's boom-and-bust budgeting. Voting YES on Proposition 2 will:
DOUBLE THE STATE'S RESERVE REQUIREMENT-from 10 to 20 percent of General Fund revenues-so California has a real cushion, not a token one, when the next downturn hits.
STOP SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-When tax revenues spike, this measure forces politicians to budget smarter by requiring the state to bank more of that windfall instead of committing it to new ongoing spending California can't sustain.
GUARANTEE EDUCATION FUNDING IS PROTECTED IN THE STATE CONSTITUTION, even as reserves grow.
INCREASE FINANCIAL SECURITY-As Washington moves to cut billions in health care and food assistance funding, this measure will ensure California is better prepared to absorb those losses without slashing the programs Californians depend on.
This is not a partisan idea. Republicans and Democrats in the state Legislature and Governor Gavin Newsom support Proposition 2.
California's own nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require. Proposition 2 follows that advice.
Please join the California Professional Firefighters, small business organizations, and former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra in supporting Proposition 2 because they see, firsthand, what happens when reserves run dry: healthcare clinics closed, schools defunded, essential services cut, and fire protection slashed.
Saving for a rainy day is what California families do. It's what California's state government should do too. Vote YES on Proposition 2-and make sure the next time the economy turns, California is ready.
Learn more at YesOnProp2.com .
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Jesse Gabriel , Chair
California State Assembly Budget Committee
Maria S. Salinas , CEO
Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 2
The supporters of Proposition 2 want you to believe this measure is about fiscal responsibility and protecting funding for education, public safety, and healthcare. Within 24 hours of introducing this measure, many of the same politicians who praised it as a way to build reserves also supported legislation to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits into the state’s savings account. Proposition 2 asks Californians to double the size of the savings account while making it less likely that taxpayers will receive the rebates they are constitutionally owed.
PROP. 2 MAKES TAXPAYER REBATES LESS LIKELY
State revenues that exceed constitutional spending limits must be returned to taxpayers. Proposition 2 creates a loophole, allowing politicians to shift billions into reserve accounts that no longer count towards the spending limit, making your rebate far less likely.
PROP. 2 DOES NOT GUARANTEE ANY NEW FUNDING FOR HEALTHCARE, EDUCATION OR PUBLIC SAFETY
Supporters claim Prop. 2 will protect education, healthcare, and public safety. Currently, it doesn’t dedicate any new dollars to any of those priorities. Sacramento politicians will continue to decide how much to spend each year, not you. Prop. 2 only allows for politicians to spend more on pet projects.
Sacramento doesn’t need another budget gimmick or wasteful spending. It needs the discipline to live within the constitutional limits that voters have already approved.
Vote NO on Proposition 2.
David Tangipa , Vice Chair
Assembly Budget Committee
Carl DeMaio , Chairman
Reform California
Steven Choi , Vice Chair
Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendments Committee
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 2
Voting NO on Prop. 2 means more money in your pocket- and less wasteful spending!
PROP. 2 CREATES A SLUSH FUND FOR SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS
In 1978 California voters overwhelmingly voted to amend the state constitution to impose a spending limit on state politicians-and the politicians have hated that spending limit ever since. Prop. 2 allows the politicians to gut the voter-imposed spending limit. What the politicians dishonestly call a “rainy day fund” is actually a SLUSH FUND! Politicians can raid this new slush fund to feed their runaway spending habits.
PROP. 2 CANCELS YOUR TAX REBATE
California already has the highest taxes in the nation, but the state constitution requires that a tax rebate be provided to you when revenues exceed the spending limit. Prop. 2 creates loopholes and accounting gimmicks so politicians can eliminate any chance of you getting your tax rebate.
PROP. 2 ALLOWS FOR MORE WASTEFUL SPENDING
California’s state budget has grown by 76% since 2018-and the size of state government has mushroomed by 40% even after adjusting for inflation! Do you feel like you are getting 40% more services and benefits today than you did in 2018? Of course not! In fact, many core services to citizens have been gutted. We’re spending more, but getting less.
That’s because state politicians have diverted your tax dollars to boondoggle projects and no-bid contracts that reward their campaign contributors. Of the little money spent on important programs, too much of it is being lost because of fraud and wasteful spending. By eliminating the spending limit on politicians we will see even more wasteful spending.
PROP. 2 MAKES OUR BUDGET MORE VOLATILE
When times are good, the state is supposed to set money aside so families and businesses are not hit with tax increases, cuts to essential services, or budget chaos during the next economic downturn. Sacramento doesn’t need a new tool to save money. It needs the discipline to follow the rules already in place and stop spending money it doesn’t have. Prop. 2 makes our budget more volatile- putting us at greater risk of a financial crisis.
PROP. 2 IS OPPOSED BY TRUSTED BUDGET WATCHDOGS
Take a look at who is supporting Prop. 2: politicians who have repeatedly mismanaged our budget and special interests that get government contracts! Within 24 hours of putting it on the ballot, the politicians backing Prop. 2 voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits into the state’s budget reserve. In contrast, opponents of Prop. 2 are government accountability and transparency watchdogs-including the Reform California and the Transparency Foundation. Californians do not need another budget gimmick dressed up as reform. We need honest budgeting, reform of wasteful spending, and a real spending limit to hold politicians accountable.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 2.
David Tangipa , Vice Chair
Assembly Budget Committee
Steven Choi , Vice Chair
Senate Elections and Constitutional Amendment Committee
Carl DeMaio , Chairman
Reform California
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 2
PROPOSITION 2 PROTECTS CALIFORNIANS FROM BOOM-AND-BUST BUDGETS
Opponents say the state needs “discipline,” not a new tool. But relying on their definition of “discipline” alone gave California a $100 billion surplus followed by a $50 billion deficit-exactly the boom-and-bust cycle Proposition 2 is designed to prevent. That instability, not this measure, is what leads to layoffs, healthcare cuts, slashed services, and tax hikes.
STOPS SACRAMENTO POLITICIANS FROM OVERSPENDING-Proposition 2 does not give Sacramento any new money to spend. On the contrary, it doubles the state’s reserve requirement and forces more savings-rather than new spending-when tax revenues spike.
PROTECTS SCHOOLS, PUBLIC SAFETY, AND HEALTHCARE-When the economy slows, Proposition 2 helps protect funding for schools, hospitals, health clinics, and public safety instead of placing them first in line for cuts. The theoretical “rebate” opponents refer to relies on a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving. Proposition 2 closes that loophole and mandates a real 20% Rainy Day Fund.
Don’t be fooled by those who call themselves “watchdogs.” California’s official nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office has recommended that the state expand the Rainy Day Fund to prevent boom-and-bust budget cycles. That’s why Proposition 2 is backed by the California Professional Firefighters, small business advocates, health clinics, hospitals, and education leaders-people who understand what happens when reserves run dry.
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 2- www.YesonProp2.com
Dr. Linda Darling-Hammond , President
California State Board of Education
Carmela Coyle , CEO
California Hospital Association
Francisco J. Silva , CEO
California Primary Care Association

Gov. Gavin Newsom presents his revised 2025-26 budget proposal in Sacramento on May 14, 2025.
Proponents say Prop. 2 would allow the state to shore up its reserves for an economic downturn. Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future.
The question Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/) poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?
The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260aca20), seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.
It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.
Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.
Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle (https://calmatters.org/explainers/california-budget-whiplash/) at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/05/gavin-newsom-final-budget-plan/) to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.
Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups (https://www.yesonprop2.com/#endorsements), including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.
“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/rainy-day-fund-california-proposition/) Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/jesse-gabriel-160858), an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/josh-hoover-165420), a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue. Proposition 2 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-2-rainy-day-fund/), or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays (https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/el-nino-long-irs-tax-deadline-delays) triggered by natural disasters. Will Californians vote to save more tax revenue in rainy day fund?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California’s booming stock market is bringing in billions of dollars in unexpected tax revenue.

Proposition 2, or the Save for California’s Future Act, aims to shore up the state’s rainy day fund by allowing state leaders to save up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue, up from the current ceiling of 10%. 

The state would also be required to save more when revenue is growing faster, and allow state lawmakers to use some of it to pay down California’s $20 billion in federal unemployment insurance debt. 

Supporters say saving more now would help the state weather a future economic downturn. 

California has been stuck in a boom-or-bust state budget cycle because its tax revenue depends heavily on wealthy residents’ stock market earnings. Some economists have warned the current economic boom may not last, and the state could face deeper budget uncertainties due to federal budget cuts and potential tax filing delays triggered by natural disasters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic legislators spearheaded Prop. 2, which is also endorsed by labor unions, chambers of commerce and a coalition of advocates for healthcare, housing and transit. 

“If you don’t have a rainy day fund, then what happens is you get forced to contemplate cuts to core essential services,” said Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat.

But opponents, including most Republican lawmakers, say saving more would only embolden legislators to spend more. The state should refund taxpayers during a good year, not set the money aside, they argue.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

California leaders and voters have historically established reserves several times, but always quickly withdrew all the funds during budget crises. In 2014, voters approved a law that required the state to save more aggressively and made it harder to withdraw money. 

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year for reserves and paying down debts. State lawmakers are allowed to withdraw up to half the balance from the reserves when the governor declares and the Legislature ratifies a budget emergency, unless they’ve already done that the previous year and the emergency remains. There are no limits on what lawmakers can spend the money on.

Prop. 2 would keep those rules and allow the state to save more. Critics say state leaders have too much leeway in spending the money. 

David Crane, a former economic adviser to former Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, said the rules let “governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

5. No new taxes, no new spending; merely reallocates surplus revenues that would otherwise count toward the Gann limit / be subject to refund calculations.
6. Support from the LA Chamber of Commerce, the California Professional Firefighters, the California Hospital Association, and both parties (one Republican, Josh Hoover, supports it).
7. The current reserve level of about $20 billion (10% of GF taxes) is considered too small for a state with this degree of revenue volatility.

Pro-NO:
1. The Gann limit (Prop 111) refund provision: by excluding reserve deposits from the spending cap (and counting them upon withdrawal), the measure reduces the likelihood that taxpayer refunds are actually triggered. Refunds have hardly been paid since 1999 (the last refund was in 1999, and the mechanism has largely been a "paper refund" — refunds have rarely been triggered because expenditures are structured to come in under the cap). Opponents (Reform California, Transparency Foundation, most Republicans) argue that this is a constitutional spending limit loophole.
2. There's no new dedicated funding for schools/healthcare/public safety — that's an argument about the intent of the funding, not about actual new dedicated funds.
3. Credibility concern: the legislature, right after introducing the measure, voted to suspend $5 billion in required BSA deposits (2025-26?), showing they'll spend the surplus rather than save it.
4. No new restrictions on how the reserve is spent (unrestricted funds); the governor can always draw from the reserves.
5. David Crane's critique: the governor can bake in optimistic spending.

Now, the user is asking for a yes/no recommendation. Let me think about which side is substantively more defensible.

Core question: Is the rainy day fund (reserve) useful, or is it a slush fund that enables more spending?

Evidence that the rainy day fund is useful:
- California's revenue volatility is among the highest of any US state (the share of capital gains in revenue is huge). The 2022-2024 experience: a $100 billion surplus followed by a ~$50 billion deficit. With a larger reserve, the state could have weathered the downturn with smaller cuts.
- The LAO (nonpartisan) has recommended larger reserves. The LAO analysis says reserves "somewhat ease budget balancing when revenues decline."
- The measure mandates saving (1.5% base + additional during capital gains booms) until the fund reaches 20% of General Fund taxes — this is a mandatory saving requirement, not discretionary. Actually wait — is that really true? Under current law, the 1.5% deposit is mandatory. The measure keeps the mandatory deposit and raises the cap from 10% to 20%, so deposits continue until the fund hits 20%. Also, it expands the additional capital-gains deposit (100% of growth between 8-10%, 150% above 10% growth).
- Extending additional debt payments to 2040 reduces future pension liabilities and can be used to pay down federal UI debt (~$20 billion) — saving interest costs.

Evidence that it's harmful:
- Exemption from the Gann limit: this is a real constitutional change that weakens the 1978 spending cap. In practice, however, refunds under the Gann limit have been largely theoretical — the last actual refund was in 1999 (the 1999-2000 tax rebate of about $1.9 billion? Actually the last refund was in 1999). Since then, the cap has not been triggered because the legislature sets spending below the cap, and the "refund" has been a mechanism that effectively returns the money to the state's own budget. Hmm, actually there's a subtle point: the Gann limit refund applies to "general fund taxes above a certain threshold"... The mechanism: if spending exceeds the limit, the excess must be returned to taxpayers as a rebate. Since 1999, this has almost never been triggered, and opponents argue that exempting deposits from the cap is a loophole that makes refunds less likely. Proponents counter that the "refund" is itself an accounting gimmick.

The "refund" point is really the crux of the argument. Is the Gann limit refund a real right of taxpayers that the measure erodes? In practice, the Gann limit refund has not been paid since 1999, and the excess above the cap has effectively flowed back to the state (the "refund" is... let me think. Under Prop 111, if spending exceeds the cap, the excess revenue is returned to taxpayers as a rebate. But in practice, the legislature has set the spending cap such that it wasn't triggered. Actually, there's a subtlety: the cap is set at a level that accounts for the reserve... In recent years, when revenues spiked (2022), was there a Gann limit refund? I think the 2021-22 budget had an issue where the state didn't trigger the Gann limit refund because... hmm. I recall a 2022-23 controversy: when the state had a $100 billion surplus, the Gann limit required the state to... Actually, the state calculated the Gann limit refund as "negative" — that is, the state was "owed" a refund (the "refunds due to the state" mechanism). There's a mechanism where, in boom years, the Gann limit generates a "refund" to the state itself (because spending is below the cap, and that excess is... no wait, that's wrong).

Let me be careful: Prop 111 (Gann limit, 1978) states that the state's appropriations from the General Fund shall not exceed the limit. If the state does exceed it, the excess must be returned to taxpayers as a rebate. In practice, the cap is set high enough that it is never triggered, and there's also a mechanism that, in years when the state's actual revenue is below the cap, generates a "refund" to the state budget (which gets added to available funds). In any case, the refund to taxpayers hasn't been paid since 1999.

So the practical effect of the Gann limit exemption: it allows the state to put more money into reserves without counting it as "spending" toward the cap, which means (a) the state can accumulate reserves that can be used for any purpose later, (b) it doesn't reduce the likelihood of a refund to taxpayers that would have occurred in the first place (since a refund hasn't been triggered in 25+ years), (c) it also means the state's "excess above the cap" calculation changes.

Given the reality that no refund to taxpayers has been triggered since 1999, the "refund" argument is more about principle than about actual lost money. Meanwhile, the benefits of a larger reserve are real: California has experienced exactly the kind of boom-bust whiplash that the reserve is designed to mitigate, and the LAO has recommended a larger reserve. Also, the federal cuts to Medi-Cal (Medi-Cal cuts in the 2025 federal budget) create new pressure on the state's budget; having a larger cushion helps avoid cuts to schools (Prop 98 funding is protected) and healthcare.

One more consideration: the measure is a constitutional amendment (simple majority), passed the legislature 29-2 in the Senate and 59-8 in the Assembly — broad support.

Another angle: the "suspension of $5 billion in required deposits" — I should verify what that refers to. In the 2025-26 budget (or the 2024-25 budget), the state suspended the mandatory BSA deposit and used the money for other things (e.g., the 2025 budget used $5 billion... hmm). Actually, I think in the 2025 revised budget, the governor and legislature suspended the 1.5% BSA deposit... The rebuttal claims that "within 24 hours of introducing the measure, the same politicians who had praised it also supported legislation suspending over $5 billion in required deposits to the state's reserve account." The introduction was around June 2026 (ACA 20, 2026 Statutes Chapter 130, June 2026). Hmm, that's the 2026 budget... The claim: in the 2025-26 budget, California suspended BSA deposits? I recall that the 2024-25 budget had a provision suspending the BSA deposit... Let me search and verify.

Also, there's an important nuance: the 2014 Proposition 2 already allows the governor to suspend deposits during a budget emergency. In the 2023-24 budget, the state suspended... Actually, during the 2023-24 budget emergency, the state did not take from the BSA but stopped... hmm.

I think I have enough information to make a well-reasoned call, but let me verify the $5 billion deposit suspension claim and get the CalMatters voter guide's "what it means" plus the LAO PDF for the details of the Gann limit provision. Let me also check the rest of the IJPR article.

content.text:
ican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

Proposition 2
Raise limit on rainy day fund deposits
This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. The deposits would not count toward the voter-approved Gann Limit, which caps the amount state lawmakers can spend each year and requires excess funds to be returned to the people. It also authorizes spending some tax revenue to pay down California’s $20 billion federal unemployment insurance debt. The California Legislature placed this measure on the ballot.

Support
California’s tax revenue is volatile and relies heavily on the stock market. Supporters say raising the ceiling would allow the state to save more when the economy is booming, building a stronger reserve for economic downturns.

content.text:
ican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.
“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/279785#t=685&f=074f023444d682ecc1d857e24642a263) Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican.
How long have we had a rainy day fund?
Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5028) to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.
In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-feb-10-me-dems10-story.htm) that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.
But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees (https://web.archive.org/web/20090809224605/http://www.dpa.ca.gov/news/news/2008/20081106-01.htm) and delayed payments (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2018/3910/recession-recovery-121318.pdf) to schools and local governments.
In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.
“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed (https://www.sfgate.com/politics/article/Jerry-Brown-preaches-for-Prop-2-by-talking-up-5812922.php) stumping for the reform.
The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.
Under the law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division&title&part&chapter&article=XVI), state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.
A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.
Bigger reserve = more to spend?
Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.
“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane (https://sfstandard.com/opinion/2026/09/14/newsom-rainy-day-fund-prop-2/), a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse (https://calmatters.org/politics/2022/08/california-campaign-finance-donor-network/) that aims to “counter special interest influence.”
“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”
In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.
“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Now I have a comprehensive overall picture. Let me organize the key facts:

**What Proposition 2 (November 3, 2026) does:**
1. Doubles the cap on the BSA (Budget Stabilization Account, the "rainy day fund") from 10% to 20% of General Fund tax revenue, requiring deposits to continue until the fund reaches 20%.
2. Requires larger additional deposits when capital gains revenue growth is high (100% of growth from 8–10%, 150% of growth above 10% — from the ABGT analysis).
3. Extends the additional debt-payment requirement from 2030 to 2040, and broadens the scope of what those payments can cover (pension/retiree healthcare debt, school payments, inter-fund borrowings, federal unemployment insurance (UI) loans — California has roughly $20 billion in UI debt).
4. Exempts BSA deposits from the Gann limit (Prop 111, 1978); they count against the limit only when withdrawn. Same treatment for the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (PSSSA), capped at 10% of General Fund tax revenue.
5. No new taxes; no new dedicated spending. LAO's fiscal findings: reserves will grow; debt payments may increase.
6. The legislature passed it 29-2 in the Senate and 59-8 in the Assembly (June 2026). Effective for the January 2027 budget (FY 2027-28).

**Context / Track record:**
- California's revenue is extremely volatile (capital gains). In 2022 there was a $100 billion surplus, followed by a roughly $50 billion deficit in 2023-24. During FY 2024-25 and 2025-26, the state withdrew about $12.2 billion from the BSA and suspended deposits (including $5.4 billion in "true-up" deposits for 2025-26). BSA balance: $15.1 billion heading into 2026-27 (10% of General Fund tax revenue = cap; so the fund is at the cap and deposits stop unless it's withdrawn).
- The claim that "the same politicians suspended $5 billion in deposits within 24 hours" is factually accurate (per the California Today guide, the budget that was chaperoned June 29, four days after ACA 20 was passed on June 25, suspended the $5.4 billion true-up deposit). Note the nuance: suspensions are allowed during budget emergencies under the 2014 law; the state declared a budget emergency in response to the projected 2025-26 deficit. So the suspension was a use of the existing emergency authority, not an evasion of the 2014 rules.
- The LAO (nonpartisan) has long recommended that the state save more than current rules require; the measure follows that advice.
- Historical pattern: before 2014, reserves were repeatedly drained in crises (2008-09: deep cuts, furloughs, delayed payments to schools). The 2014 Proposition 2 (70% approval) strengthened the rules.
- Opponents' main argument: the Gann limit exemption weakens the voter-approved spending cap and reduces the possibility of taxpayer rebates; reserves are a "slush fund" with broad withdrawal authority; no new dedicated funding for the programs the supporters mention.
- Proponents' rebuttal: rebates haven't actually been paid out since 1979 (the last was 1999… let me verify: under the Gann limit, rebates have… actually, I think the last actual Gann limit rebate to taxpayers was 1999-2000 ($1.9 billion? hmm). Let me be careful. In practice, I recall the last Gann limit refund was paid in 1999. The mechanism has effectively been dormant since. In boom years (2021-22), the state actually had "negative rebates" (rebates to the state). So the practical impact of the exemption on rebates to taxpayers is minimal, but in principle it changes the accounting.

**Who supports/opposes:**
- Support: Governor Newsom, Legislative Democrats, California Professional Firefighters, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, California Hospital Association, California State Board of Education, former HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra, one Republican (Josh Hoover). Media: Sacramento Bee, San Francisco Chronicle.
- Opposition: Legislative Republicans (majority), Carl DeMaio, David Tangipa, Steven Choi, Reform California, Transparency Foundation, Howard Jarvis? (not listed), former Schwarzenegger adviser David Crane. Media: San Diego Union-Tribune, Orange County Register.

**My analysis for the judgment:**

The core question: is a bigger mandatory rainy-day fund good fiscal policy for California?

Arguments in favor of YES:
1. California's revenue volatility is extreme and structurally tied to stock market wealth effects. A 10% cap is clearly too low: the state hit the cap and stopped saving while revenues were at historic highs, and then the subsequent deficit forced $12.2 billion in withdrawals + deposit suspensions. A 20% cap means the state would have had to save more during the AI-fueled boom years of 2025-26.
2. This is a mandatory saving requirement, not a discretionary "slush fund": it requires annual deposits until 20% of General Fund tax revenue is reached, with even larger deposits during capital gains booms. The only discretionary parts are the existing ones (suspension/withdrawal during budget emergencies — unchanged by this measure).
3. Extending the debt payments to 2040 reduces long-term pension/UI liabilities and saves interest — a direct fiscal benefit, including paying down the $20 billion federal UI debt.
4. The nonpartisan LAO has recommended larger reserves.
5. Federal funding cuts (Medi-Cal, food assistance) increase the risk of future deficits; larger reserves mean less whiplash from cuts to schools (Prop 98), healthcare, and public safety.
6. The withdrawal rules aren't changed — the same 2014 rules apply.
7. No new taxes.

Arguments in favor of NO:
1. The Gann limit exemption is a real weakening of a voter-approved spending cap (though rebates haven't actually been paid out since 1999, so the real-world impact is minor; the "rebate" is an accounting mechanism that has never functioned as designed).
2. The 2014 history shows the legislature will suspend deposits and withdraw funds when convenient (2024-26) — the track record suggests future governors will raid a bigger fund too. David Crane's critique is legitimate: the withdrawal trigger (shortfall vs. spending in the past three budget years) is easy to trigger.
3. No new dedicated funding for schools/healthcare/public safety (the supporters' framing overstates this).
4. The timing optics: the legislature passed the "save more" measure and then in the same budget cycle suspended a $5.4 billion deposit to cover a deficit.

Weighing these: the NO arguments are primarily principle/credibility-based (spending cap, "they'll raid it"), whereas the YES arguments are practical (demonstrated revenue volatility, demonstrated 2022-26 whiplash, nonpartisan LAO recommendation, long-term debt reduction). The Gann limit rebate mechanism has been essentially a phantom right for decades — no actual rebates to taxpayers since 1999, so the claim that "this measure steals your rebate" is largely rhetorical. In fact, wait — I should double-check the last Gann limit rebate. I think the last actual Gann limit refund to taxpayers was 1999 (the "Prop 111 refund" of about $1.9 billion was paid in the 1999-2000 budget year?). Hmm. I'm fairly confident the mechanism hasn't triggered taxpayer rebates in the 2000s-2020s, because the legislature sets appropriations below the limit. There were some small "rebates"… actually no — in recent years, the excess over the Gann limit has been… let me not overstate this. I could do a quick search to verify the last Gann limit refund year.

Also worth noting: the measure was passed with a large majority (59-8, 29-2) and has bipartisan support (at least one Republican). 2014's Proposition 2 passed 70-30. The 2004 Proposition 58 also passed (by about 60%?). Voters have a history of supporting reserve building.

One more point in favor of YES: even opponents acknowledge reserves are needed; the debate is over size and the spending-cap exemption. A 20% reserve cap is roughly… let me calculate: 20% of General Fund tax revenue. General Fund tax revenue is about $160-170 billion? The state is projected to spend $250 billion from the General Fund. 10% of General Fund tax revenue ≈ $15 billion (per the budget center, the BSA at the cap is $15.1 billion). So 20% ≈ $30 billion. That's a reasonable level — comparable to what many states with volatile revenue hold. Actually, the LAO has historically recommended the state hold reserves equal to 1-2 quarters of spending… the state's own May 2026 revision projects $29.9 billion in reserves — i.e., the state itself is heading toward about 20% under current rules. So Proposition 2 merely constitutionalizes what the state would do anyway in good years.

Given all this, my judgment: YES.

Rationale:
- The practical case for a larger buffer is strong and nonpartisan (the LAO recommends it; California's demonstrated $100 billion → $50 billion whiplash; federal cuts add risk).
- The measure is a mandatory saving requirement (deposit until 20% is reached), not new discretionary spending; no new taxes.
- The debt extension saves long-term costs (pension, federal UI debt).
- The main NO argument (Gann limit rebate) is largely theoretical — the rebate mechanism has effectively not paid out to taxpayers in about 25 years; and the withdrawal rules remain as voters approved them in 2014.
- The "credibility" criticism (suspended $5.4 billion in deposits) is real, but the suspension was a use of the existing 2014 emergency authority during an actual budget emergency — and importantly, even with those withdrawals and suspensions, the BSA balance rose from $11.2 billion to $15.1 billion.

Let me do one final verification search on the last Gann limit refund, to make sure my "the rebate is a phantom" claim is accurate. Also, the California Budget Center's "Should Voters Approve Proposition 2" page may have a balanced analysis I should read. Let me do those two fetches, and then write my answer.
I'll verify the history of Gann Limit rebates and check the California Budget Center's analysis before finalizing my response.

- Opponents' main argument: the Gann limit exemption weakens the voter-approved spending cap and reduces the possibility of taxpayer rebates; reserves are a "slush fund" with broad withdrawal authority; no new dedicated funding for the programs the supporters mention.
- Proponents' rebuttal: rebates haven't actually been paid out since 1979 (the last was 1999… let me verify: under the Gann limit, rebates have… actually, I think the last actual Gann limit rebate to taxpayers was 1999-2000 ($1.9 billion? hmm). Let me be careful. In practice, I recall the last Gann limit refund was paid in 1999. The mechanism has effectively been dormant since. In boom years (2021-22), the state actually had "negative rebates" (rebates to the state). So the practical impact of the exemption on rebates to taxpayers is minimal, but in principle it changes the accounting.

**Who supports/opposes:**
- Support: Governor Newsom, Legislative Democrats, California Professional Firefighters, LA Area Chamber of Commerce, California Hospital Association, California State Board of Education, former HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra, one Republican (Josh Hoover). Media: Sacramento Bee, San Francisco Chronicle.
- Opposition: Legislative Republicans (majority), Carl DeMaio, David Tangipa, Steven Choi, Reform California, Transparency Foundation, Howard Jarvis? (not listed), former Schwarzenegger adviser David Crane. Media: San Diego Union-Tribune, Orange County Register.

**My analysis for the judgment:**

The core question: is a bigger mandatory rainy-day fund good fiscal policy for California?

Arguments in favor of YES:
1. California's revenue volatility is extreme and structurally tied to stock market wealth effects. A 10% cap is clearly too low: the state hit the cap and stopped saving while revenues were at historic highs, and then the subsequent deficit forced $12.2 billion in withdrawals + deposit suspensions. A 20% cap means the state would have had to save more during the AI-fueled boom years of 2025-26.
2. This is a mandatory saving requirement, not a discretionary "slush fund": it requires annual deposits until 20% of General Fund tax revenue is reached, with even larger deposits during capital gains booms. The only discretionary parts are the existing ones (suspension/withdrawal during budget emergencies — unchanged by this measure).
3. Extending the debt payments to 2040 reduces long-term pension/UI liabilities and saves interest — a direct fiscal benefit, including paying down the $20 billion federal UI debt.
4. The nonpartisan LAO has recommended larger reserves.
5. Federal funding cuts (Medi-Cal, food assistance) increase the risk of future deficits; larger reserves mean less whiplash from cuts to schools (Prop 98), healthcare, and public safety.
6. The withdrawal rules aren't changed — the same 2014 rules apply.
7. No new taxes.

Arguments in favor of NO:
1. The Gann limit exemption is a real weakening of a voter-approved spending cap (though rebates haven't actually been paid out since 1999, so the real-world impact is minor; the "rebate" is an accounting mechanism that has never functioned as designed).
2. The 2014 history shows the legislature will suspend deposits and withdraw funds when convenient (2024-26) — the track record suggests future governors will raid a bigger fund too. David Crane's critique is legitimate: the withdrawal trigger (shortfall vs. spending in the past three budget years) is easy to trigger.
3. No new dedicated funding for schools/healthcare/public safety (the supporters' framing overstates this).
4. The timing optics: the legislature passed the "save more" measure and then in the same budget cycle suspended a $5.4 billion deposit to cover a deficit.

Weighing these: the NO arguments are primarily principle/credibility-based (spending cap, "they'll raid it"), whereas the YES arguments are practical (demonstrated revenue volatility, demonstrated 2022-26 whiplash, nonpartisan LAO recommendation, long-term debt reduction). The Gann limit rebate mechanism has been essentially a phantom right for decades — no actual rebates to taxpayers since 1999, so the claim that "this measure steals your rebate" is largely rhetorical. In fact, wait — I should double-check the last Gann limit rebate. I think the last actual Gann limit refund to taxpayers was 1999 (the "Prop 111 refund" of about $1.9 billion was paid in the 1999-2000 budget year?). Hmm. I'm fairly confident the mechanism hasn't triggered taxpayer rebates in the 2000s-2020s, because the legislature sets appropriations below the limit. There were some small "rebates"… actually no — in recent years, the excess over the Gann limit has been… let me not overstate this. I could do a quick search to verify the last Gann limit refund year.

Also worth noting: the measure was passed with a large majority (59-8, 29-2) and has bipartisan support (at least one Republican). 2014's Proposition 2 passed 70-30. The 2004 Proposition 58 also passed (by about 60%?). Voters have a history of supporting reserve building.

One more point in favor of YES: even opponents acknowledge reserves are needed; the debate is over size and the spending-cap exemption. A 20% reserve cap is roughly… let me calculate: 20% of General Fund tax revenue. General Fund tax revenue is about $160-170 billion? The state is projected to spend $250 billion from the General Fund. 10% of General Fund tax revenue ≈ $15 billion (per the budget center, the BSA at the cap is $15.1 billion). So 20% ≈ $30 billion. That's a reasonable level — comparable to what many states with volatile revenue hold. Actually, the LAO has historically recommended the state hold reserves equal to 1-2 quarters of spending… the state's own May 2026 revision projects $29.9 billion in reserves — i.e., the state itself is heading toward about 20% under current rules. So Proposition 2 merely constitutionalizes what the state would do anyway in good years.

Given all this, my judgment: YES.

Rationale:
- The practical case for a larger buffer is strong and nonpartisan (the LAO recommends it; California's demonstrated $100 billion → $50 billion whiplash; federal cuts add risk).
- The measure is a mandatory saving requirement (deposit until 20% is reached), not new discretionary spending; no new taxes.
- The debt extension saves long-term costs (pension, federal UI debt).
- The main NO argument (Gann limit rebate) is largely theoretical — the rebate mechanism has effectively not paid out to taxpayers in about 25 years; and the withdrawal rules remain as voters approved them in 2014.
- The "credibility" criticism (suspended $5.4 billion in deposits) is real, but the suspension was a use of the existing 2014 emergency authority during an actual budget emergency — and importantly, even with those withdrawals and suspensions, the BSA balance rose from $11.2 billion to $15.1 billion.

Let me do one final verification search on the last Gann limit refund, to make sure my "the rebate is a phantom" claim is accurate. Also, the California Budget Center's "Should Voters Approve Proposition 2" page may have a balanced analysis I should read. Let me do those two fetches, and then write my answer.

Issue Brief
Should Voters Approve Proposition 2? How California’s Rainy Day Fund Would Be Updated
Examining the 2026 Ballot Measure to Strengthen California’s Budget Stabilization Account and Modify the Gann Limit
August 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Erik Saucedo
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 2 on the November 2026 ballot would change the rules for California’s rainy day fund to build a larger reserve and better protect core public services during budget emergencies, such as an economic downturn. Prop. 2 also would expand the types of state debt that could be repaid with General Fund revenues that must be set aside each year. In addition, Prop. 2 would modify the relationship between certain reserves and California’s state spending cap, or “Gann Limit” — a change that would allow policymakers to build up reserves in years when revenues are strong and the state is at risk of exceeding the limit. The Legislature placed Prop. 2, a constitutional amendment, on the ballot by passing ACA 20 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260ACA20).
table of contents
What Would Proposition 2 Do?
What Would Proposition 2 Not Do?
What Would Proposition 2 Mean for California?
What Would Proposition 2 Do?
Prop. 2 would amend the state Constitution to change several of the rules that govern California’s rainy day fund — the state’s primary budget reserve, known as the Budget Stabilization Account (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/) (BSA). 1 (javascript:void(0)) California voters created the BSA in 2004 by passing Prop. 58 and reformed the BSA a decade later by approving Prop. 2 of 2014. For an analysis of Prop. 2 of 2014, see California Budget & Policy Center, Proposition 2: Should California Prioritize Paying Down Debt and Significantly Change State Budget Reserve Policies? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf) (September 2014). In addition, Prop. 2 would modestly change the interaction between state reserves and the state spending cap, commonly called the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). This section highlights the key changes that Prop. 2 would make if approved by voters in November.
Increases the Maximum Size of the Rainy Day Fund (BSA) to 20% of General Fund Revenues
Current Law
The state Constitution limits the size of the BSA to 10% of estimated General Fund tax revenues. 2 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, the amount transferred to the BSA in any fiscal year may not result in a balance that exceeds 10% of estimated General Fund “proceeds of taxes.” Proceeds of taxes are estimated for the purpose of calculating the State Appropriations Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/4416) (or Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/)) and tend to differ slightly from total General Fund revenues and transfers. When this limit is reached, any dollars that otherwise would go into the BSA must be spent on infrastructure.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would double the BSA cap to 20% of estimated General Fund tax revenues. If the 20% cap were ever reached, the dollars that would otherwise be deposited into the BSA would instead be spent on infrastructure, as under current law.
Changes How “Excess” Capital Gains Revenues Are Calculated to Save More in Strong Revenue Years
Current Law
The state Constitution requires some General Fund revenues to be set aside annually and requires additional General Fund revenues to be set aside when certain conditions are met. Generally speaking, 50% of these set-aside revenues are deposited into the rainy day fund, and the other 50% are used to pay down certain state debts. 3 (javascript:void(0)) As noted below, some set-aside revenues are owed to TK-14 education through the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. This portion of set-aside revenues is governed by different rules and does not go toward the rainy day fund or state debt payments. These set-aside revenues are determined in two ways:
1.5% of General Fund revenues are automatically set aside every year. For example, if General Fund tax revenues were estimated to total $250 billion for a fiscal year, the state would need to set aside a total of $3.75 billion (1.5%), with half deposited into the rainy day fund (BSA) and the other half used to pay down certain state debts. Prop. 2 would not change this required annual transfer.
In addition to this fixed annual transfer, the state is required to set aside “excess” capital gains revenues. This requirement is triggered in years when estimated General Fund tax revenues that come from personal income taxes on capital gains exceed a specified target: 8% of total General Fund tax revenues. 4 (javascript:void(0)) Capital gains are the profits realized from selling assets that have increased in value, such as stock shares or real estate. Revenues from capital gains can be volatile from year to year depending on market conditions. When this occurs, a portion of these “excess” capital gains revenues — specifically, the share that is not owed to TK-14 education through the Proposition 98 minimum funding guarantee (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/what-is-proposition-98-guaranteed-school-funding-explained/) — is split equally between building the BSA balance and paying down certain state debts. 5 (javascript:void(0)) The share of “excess” capital gains revenues that are owed to TK-14 education via Prop. 98 is subject to a different set of rules. See California Budget & Policy Center, Proposition 2: Should California Prioritize Paying Down Debt and Significantly Change State Budget Reserve Policies? (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf) (September 2014), p. 2.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would change how “excess” capital gains revenues are calculated in order to set aside more revenue for the rainy day fund and state debt payments. Under Prop. 2, there would be two categories of “excess” capital gains revenues, as follows:
The first category of “excess” revenues would include capital gains revenues that total between 8% and 10% of General Fund tax revenues.
The second category of “excess” revenues would equal 1.5 times the portion of capital gains revenues that are above 10% of General Fund tax revenues. For example, if there are $2 billion in capital gains revenues above the 10% threshold, the state would have to set aside a total of $3 billion ($2.0 billion * 1.5) — $1 billion more than is required under current law.
As under current law, the portion of these “excess” revenues that are not owed to TK-14 education through Prop. 98 would be split equally between the rainy day fund and certain state debt payments.
Expands the Types of State Debt That May Be Paid with Set-Aside Revenues
Current Law
The state Constitution requires that half of General Fund revenues set aside each year be used to repay certain state debts. 6 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues used to calculate this 50% requirement exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Currently, the state may only use these set-aside revenues to 1) prefund state retiree health benefits and/or 2) pay down unfunded liabilities associated with state‑level pension plans. In prior years, the state was allowed to use these set-aside revenues to pay down certain types of budgetary debt . This included payments owed to K-12 schools and community colleges as of July 1, 2014. 7 (javascript:void(0)) These payments went toward unfunded prior-year Prop. 98 obligations, including so-called “settle-up” obligations, which reflect the reconciliation of estimates of the annual Prop. 98 minimum funding level and the actual Prop. 98 guarantee. However, by 2019-20, the state had repaid all of the outstanding budgetary debt (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4887).
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would update and expand the list of state debts that could be paid with set-aside revenues. Specifically, these funds could be used to:
Repay federal unemployment insurance (UI) loans. Under Prop. 2, revenues set aside for state debt could be used to repay “federal loans made to the Unemployment Fund.” The measure does not specify whether Prop. 2 funds could be used to pay the interest as well as the principal on federal UI loans.
Repay certain TK-14 education obligations. Under Prop. 2, the state could once again use set-aside revenues, during any fiscal year, to make certain payments owed to TK-12 schools and community colleges. 8 (javascript:void(0)) Specifically, Prop. 2 would allow revenues set aside for state debt payments to be used for “unfunded prior fiscal year General Fund obligations” pursuant to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. These include so-called “settle-up” obligations, which reflect the reconciliation of estimates of the annual Prop. 98 minimum funding level and the actual Prop. 98 guarantee. Under the original Prop. 2 (2014 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/2022/10/Prop-2-2020-IB.pdf)), the state was allowed to use set-aside revenues to pay down unfunded prior fiscal year General Fund obligations pursuant to Prop. 98, but only for debt accrued prior to July 1, 2014. That debt was repaid by the 2019-20 fiscal year. In addition, set-aside revenues could be used to help accelerate the phase-out of an outstanding debt tied to an accounting maneuver that state leaders adopted in the 2023-24 budget (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) to address an issue related to the Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For a discussion of this accounting maneuver, see Legislative Analyst’s Office, The 2024-25 Budget: The Governor’s Proposition 98 Funding Maneuver (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4840) (February 15, 2024).
Repay General Fund loans to the Medi-Cal program. The 2025-26 budget transferred $4.4 billion (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5075) from the state General Fund to the Medical Providers Interim Payment Fund (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/0201) to help cover higher-than-expected Medi-Cal costs. The budget delayed repayment of this loan, with payments starting in 2027-28 and potentially continuing for several years. Under Prop. 2, revenues set aside for state debt could be used to accelerate the paydown of the 2025-26 Medi-Cal loan or other Medi-Cal loans.
Extends the Debt-Paydown Requirement by 10 Years, to 2039-40
Current Law
The state Constitution requires 50% of set-aside revenues to be used to pay down certain state debts through the 2029-30 state fiscal year. 10 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues used to calculate this 50% requirement exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Starting in 2030-31, these payments become optional, and any set-aside revenues that are not used to pay down debt must be deposited into the rainy day fund.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would require 50% of set-aside revenues to go toward paying down state debts for an additional 10 years ending in 2039-40. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The revenues that would be used to calculate this 50% requirement would continue to exclude set-aside revenues that are owed to TK-14 education through California’s Prop. 98 minimum funding guarantee. Starting in 2040-41, these payments would become optional, and any set-aside revenues that were not used to pay down debt would have to be deposited into the rainy day fund.
Changes the Relationship Between Deposits/Withdrawals and the Gann Limit
Current Law
The state Constitution requires that deposits into state reserves be counted as spending for the purpose of calculations required by California’s spending cap. This is the case even though tax dollars transferred to a reserve clearly will not immediately be spent through the budget. This rule was put in place by Prop. 4 of 1979, which created the state spending cap. 12 (javascript:void(0)) For simplicity, this discussion uses the word “spending.” However, Prop. 4 uses the technical phrase “appropriations subject to limitation.” See California Constitution, Article XIIIB, Section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=XIII%20B). This cap is formally known as the State Appropriations Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/4416), but is more commonly called the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). 13 (javascript:void(0)) The spending cap applies to the state as well as to local governments.
In contrast, withdrawals from state reserves as well as expenditures of withdrawn funds do not count as spending for the purpose of the Gann Limit. 14 (javascript:void(0)) California Constitution, Article XIIIB, Section 5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%205.&article=XIII%20B). In other words, under current constitutional rules, tax dollars count toward the spending cap when they go into a reserve, but do not count toward the cap when they come out.
As a result, in years when state revenues are growing rapidly and the state is at risk of exceeding the spending cap, state leaders cannot bolster California’s fiscal resilience by further building up reserves, because doing so would put the state over the spending limit. 15 (javascript:void(0)) Revenues that are projected to exceed the spending limit can only be used in a few narrow ways if state leaders want to avoid going over the cap. If the state exceeds the cap for two consecutive years, half must go to taxpayers and the other half must go to TK-14 education on a per-pupil basis.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would alter the relationship between deposits/withdrawals and the Gann Limit for two state reserves: the rainy day fund (BSA) and the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account.
Prop. 2 would change the interaction between the BSA and the Gann Limit. Under Prop. 2, revenues would not count toward the state spending cap when they go into the rainy day fund, but would count when they are withdrawn.
Prop. 2 would change the interaction between the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account and the Gann Limit. The holding account (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-projected-surplus-temporary-holding-account-a-place-to-set-aside-anticipated-surplus-revenues) is used to temporarily set aside anticipated surplus revenues for up to one year. Under Prop. 2, revenues deposited into the holding account — up to a cap — would not count toward the Gann Limit, but they would count when they come out. This cap would be equal to 10% of total General Fund tax revenues in the year the transfer is made. For example, if General Fund tax revenues were estimated to total $250 billion, then up to $25 billion could go into the holding account without counting toward the Gann Limit (but would count toward the Gann Limit when withdrawn). However, if the holding account deposit exceeded $25 billion, then the excess amount would count toward the Gann Limit (but would not count when withdrawn).
Changes How a Budget Emergency May Be Declared
Current Law
The state Constitution requires the governor to declare a budget emergency in order to:
Suspend or reduce a required deposit into the rainy day fund (BSA) or the Public Schools System Stabilization Account (PSSSA), or
Withdraw funds from the BSA or the PSSSA. 16 (javascript:void(0)) For a description of the PSSSA, or schools reserve, see California Budget & Policy Center, California’s Rainy Day Fund and Other Budget Reserves Overview (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-rainy-day-fund-and-other-budget-reserves-overview/#h-public-school-system-stabilization-account-psssa-the-reserve-for-k-12-schools-amp-community-colleges) (April 2026).
To declare a budget emergency, the governor signs a proclamation. It may be signed very late in the fiscal year, including after the June 15 constitutional deadline for the Legislature to pass the budget. For example, in 2025, Governor Newsom issued a budget emergency proclamation on June 27 (https://www.gov.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Budget-Proc-2025.pdf) — well after the Legislature passed the budget and just three days before the end of the 2024-25 fiscal year.
This misaligned timing puts the Legislature in the awkward position of passing a budget that assumes a budget emergency before the governor has made it official.
Proposition 2
Prop. 2 would create a simplified pathway for declaring a budget emergency. This alternative pathway is intended to prevent a situation where the governor suggests a budget emergency will be declared, but then fails to issue a proclamation before the Legislature’s June 15 constitutional deadline to pass the budget.
Prop. 2 would allow the governor’s May Revision, which is due out by May 14, to constitute the proclamation of a budget emergency
